summary: This informational memo explains the terms and concepts used for benchmarking OSPF. It also discusses how the terms relate to the testing tasks involved, so that tests are described consistently.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4062 is a vocabulary for OSPF benchmarking. It explains where a measurement is taken, what counts as the moment a router has finished reacting to a change, and what the terms borrowed from the OSPF specification mean when they appear in a test report.

questions: what terms are used in ospf convergence tests

what does single router convergence mean
subtitle: The words used when people measure how fast an OSPF router reacts, and what each one means.

tldr.problem: Benchmark reports used the same words for different things, so two results could not be compared and a claim of conformance meant nothing.
tldr.mechanism: The memo sorts the vocabulary into three groups: how the measurement is taken, terms borrowed from OSPF itself such as the hello interval and the SPF execution time, and the meaning of convergence when only one router is being watched.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational memo that fixes no protocol and no measurement method. Its companion, RFC 4061, is where the tests themselves are described.

today: RFC 4062 is an Informational memo published in April 2005, and it has not been obsoleted or updated. It sets the vocabulary used by RFC 4061 and by the OSPF benchmarking work that followed it.

sections.title: What This Document Is For
sections.content:
RFC 4062 is a companion to RFC 4061, which describes basic OSPF testing methods. This document explains the terminology and concepts used in OSPF testing framework documents. Although some of these terms may be defined elsewhere, and the reader is referred to those definitions in some cases, the memo includes discussions concerning these terms as they relate specifically to the tasks involved in benchmarking the OSPF protocol.

As with the tests it supports, the memo uses the RFC 2119 key words to ensure methodological control, which it says is very important in the specification of benchmarks, and it notes that it does not specify a network-related protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: Benchmark reports need to mean the same thing whichever vendor wrote them. This memo is the shared dictionary that the test documents are written against.

sections.title: White Box, Black Box and Multi-Device Measurements
sections.content:
The memo starts with well-known industry and benchmarking terms that may be defined elsewhere.

White box (internal) measurements are those reported and collected on the device under test itself. They rely on output and event recording, along with the clocking and time stamping available on the device under test. Taking measurements on the device may impact the actual outcome of the test, since it can increase processor loading, memory utilization and timing factors, and some devices may not have the required output readily available for taking internal measurements. White box measurements can also be influenced by the vendor's implementation of various timers and processing models, and whenever possible internal measurements should be compared to external measurements to verify and validate them. Because of the potential for variations in collection and presentation methods across different devices, white box measurements MUST NOT be used as a basis for comparison in benchmarks. The memo says this has been a guiding principle of the Benchmarking Methodology Working Group.

Black box (external) measurements infer the performance of the device under test through observation of its communications with other devices. One example given is that when a downstream device receives complete routing information from the device under test, it can be inferred that the device under test has transmitted all the routing information available. External measurements of internal operations may suffer in that they include not just the protocol action times, but also propagation delays, queuing delays and other such factors. For the purposes of the benchmark document, external techniques are more readily applicable.

Multi-device measurements assess communications, usually in combination with internal operations, between two or more devices under test. Multi-device measurements may be internal or external.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two ways to time a router. You can read its own logs, which is accurate but changes what the router is doing while you watch, and depends on how that vendor writes its timers. Or you can watch from outside, which does not disturb the router but includes the network's own delay in the number. The memo's rule is that only the outside kind can be used to compare different products.

sections.title: Terms Borrowed from OSPF
sections.content:
The next group of terms is defined in the OSPF specification itself, and the memo includes them only as they apply to the benchmark document.

Point-to-point links are defined in section 1.2 of RFC 2328. A point-to-point link can take less time to converge than a broadcast link of the same speed, because it does not have the overhead of DR election. Point-to-point links can be either numbered or unnumbered, but in the context of the benchmark and OSPF the two can be regarded as the same.

Broadcast links are also defined in section 1.2 of RFC 2328. The adjacency formation time on a broadcast link can be greater than that on a point-to-point link of the same speed, because DR election has to take place: all routers on a broadcast network form adjacency with the DR and the BDR. Asynchronous flooding also takes place through the DR, and in the context of convergence it may take more time for an LSA to be flooded from one DR-other router to another, because the LSA first has to be processed at the DR.

Shortest Path First execution time is the time taken by a router to complete the SPF process, as described in RFC 2328. It does not include the time taken by the router to install routes in the forwarding engine. Some implementations may force two intervals, the SPF hold time and the SPF delay, between successive SPF calculations. If an SPF hold time exists it should be subtracted from the total SPF execution time, and if an SPF delay exists it should be noted in the test results. The SPF time is generally measured in milliseconds.

Hello interval is defined in section 7.1 of RFC 2328. The hello interval must be the same for all routers on a network. Decreasing the hello interval can allow the router dead interval to be reduced, thus reducing convergence times in those situations where the dead interval timing out causes an OSPF process to notice an adjacency failure.

Router dead interval is also defined in section 7.1 of RFC 2328. It is advertised in the router's Hello Packets in the Router-DeadInterval field. The router dead interval should be some multiple of the HelloInterval, perhaps four times the hello interval, and must be the same for all routers attached to a common network.
sections.plainLanguage: Two of these decide how fast a router can notice trouble. The hello interval is how often a router says hello, and the dead interval is how long it waits before deciding the neighbour has gone. Lowering the hello interval lets the dead interval be lowered too, which shortens the wait when a neighbour really has gone. The SPF execution time is the pure calculation, with the time spent installing the result in the forwarding engine left out.

sections.title: What Convergence Means Here
sections.content:
A network is termed as converged when all the devices within the network have a loop-free path to each possible destination. Because the benchmark work is not testing network convergence but testing performance for a particular device within a network, this definition has to be streamlined to fit a single device view. In that case, convergence means the point in time when the device under test has performed all the actions needed in order to react to the change in the topology represented by the test condition. For instance, an OSPF device must flood any new information it has received, rebuild its shortest path first tree, and install any new paths or destinations in the local routing information base, the RIB, or routing table.

The memo notes that the word convergence has two distinct meanings, the process of a group of individuals meeting at the same place, and the process of an individual coming to the same place as an existing group, and that this work focuses on the second meaning, so the time required for a single device to adapt to a network change is called Single Router Convergence. The concept does not include the time required for the control plane of the device to transfer the information required to forward packets to the data plane, nor the amount of time between when the data plane receives that information and when it is able to forward traffic.

Measuring convergence means there are several elements to it, even under the single device definition, including but not limited to: the time it takes for the device under test to pass the information about a network event on to its neighbours; the time it takes for the device under test to process information about a network event and to calculate a new Shortest Path Tree; and the time it takes for the device under test to make changes in its local RIB reflecting the new shortest path tree.

The memo then defines a network event as an event that causes a change in the network topology, and gives four kinds. Link or neighbor device up is the time needed for an OSPF implementation to recognize a new link coming up on the device, to build any necessary adjacencies, to synchronize its database, and to perform all other actions necessary to converge. Initialization is the time needed for an OSPF implementation to be initialized, to recognize any links across which OSPF must run, to build any needed adjacencies, to synchronize its database, and to perform other actions necessary to converge. Adjacency down is the time needed for an OSPF implementation to recognize a link down or adjacency loss based on hello timers alone, to propagate any information as necessary to its remaining adjacencies, and to perform other actions necessary to converge. Link down is the time needed for an OSPF implementation to recognize a link down based on layer 2-provided information, to propagate any information as needed to its remaining adjacencies, and to perform other actions necessary to converge.
sections.plainLanguage: Convergence here means one router has finished everything it has to do: pass the news on, work out the new paths, and put them in its routing table. It does not mean the packets have started flowing, because the forwarding side is not being measured. The four events to time are a link coming up, the router starting up, a neighbour going quiet, and a link physically failing.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The memo states in one line that it does not modify the underlying security considerations in RFC 2328.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing here changes how OSPF authenticates itself, so the rules in RFC 2328 still apply.

viz.caption: THE THREE WAYS A MEASUREMENT CAN BE TAKEN

Inferred from the device's communications with other devices

Usually a combination of the two

viz.caption: THE OSPF TERMS THE BENCHMARKS BORROW

items.title: Point-to-point link
items.text: Defined in RFC 2328. It can converge faster than a broadcast link of the same speed, because it has no DR election overhead. Numbered and unnumbered links can be treated the same.

items.title: Broadcast link
items.text: Defined in RFC 2328. Adjacency formation takes longer because a DR election has to happen first, and flooding goes through the DR.

items.title: SPF execution time
items.text: The time to complete the SPF process, not including installing the routes in the forwarding engine. Measured in milliseconds, and an SPF hold time is subtracted from it if one exists.

items.title: Hello interval
items.text: Defined in RFC 2328. Must be the same for all routers on a network. Lowering it allows the dead interval to be lowered too, which shortens convergence when a neighbour fails.

items.title: Router dead interval
items.text: Defined in RFC 2328. Advertised in the Router-DeadInterval field of the Hello Packets. It should be a multiple of the hello interval, perhaps four times, and must be the same for all routers on a common network.

viz.caption: THE THREE PARTS OF A SINGLE ROUTER CONVERGENCE

items.title: Passing it on
items.text: The time it takes for the device under test to pass the information about a network event on to its neighbours.

items.title: Working out the paths
items.text: The time it takes for the device under test to process information about a network event and to calculate a new Shortest Path Tree.

items.title: Installing the result
items.text: The time it takes for the device under test to make changes in its local RIB reflecting the new shortest path tree.
